newsitem.title: FRANCE: ONIC head satisfied with pace of EU wheat exports.
newsitem.headline: ONIC head satisfied with pace of EU wheat exports.

text.p: The head of France's cereals authority (ONIC) has said he is satisfied with the pace of European Union soft wheat exports and hopes it will be maintained despite conflicting interests facing Brussels.

"Each week the bids (for export licences) are fairly significant and, equally, the Commission is responding to them favourably," ONIC director general Alain Moulinier said in an interview on Wednesday.

While Moulinier reiterated he would like to see a faster rate of exports to meet world demand, he also said the EU was reluctant to increase current volumes because of the sudden rise in domestic prices, especially in France.
"It's clear that this rise in domestic prices is not a favourable factor for getting many certificates from Brussels," he said.
Since last Thursday French wheat for March delivery at the northern port of Rouen has climbed 12.5 French francs to 885 francs per tonne, casting a shadow over EU export willingness.
Moulinier said he thought the market was in a "sensitive period" and it would be necessary to find a balance.
"It's clear that if the French market hadn't moved at all, there would be less questioning in Brussels about giving even larger volumes," he said.

"In fact the Commission is constrained," he added, referring to last week's tender when the Commission accepted exports of 400,000 tonnes but rejected another 100,000 tonnes that would have required a fractionally higher subsidy.
"The Commission is seeing to it that domestic market prices don't take off," Moulinier said.
He said that the Commission was caught between "two contradictory imperatives" - to keep a regular flow of exports to the world market and to keep domestic prices under control.
"The Commission is faced with a balancing act which is not always easy," he said.
He said that Brussels had nonetheless managed to keep wheat refunds at "appropriate" levels despite a rise in the dollar and market prices.
Exporters have said however that refunds remain too low to allow them to fulfil large contracts with North Africa.
Moulinier declined to comment on the exporters' situation, but said "it's up to the exporters to know whether they're short (of refunds) or not."
